thread.title: Warm temperatures increase risk of bitter rot and other fruit diseases in Pennsylvania orchards
thread.title_full: Warm temperatures increase risk of bitter rot and other fruit diseases in Pennsylvania orchards

author: Keystone Today
title: Warm temperatures increase risk of bitter rot and other fruit diseases in Pennsylvania orchards
text:
Fruit growers in Pennsylvania are being advised to remain vigilant as warm temperatures and sporadic rainfall from May 28 to June 5 have created favorable conditions for bitter rot infections, according to a disease update released on May 27. The report highlights that temperature swings of up to 40 degrees over the past week have stabilized, but the threat of disease remains high due to the combination of warmth and moisture.
Growers are encouraged to review their spray records for key dates—May 20, May 25, and May 27—when conditions were suitable for bitter rot infection. The report states, “Temperatures were in the 70s, and we had at least 12 hours of leaf wetness.” Additional diseases currently affecting orchards include Marssonina blotch, sooty blotch and flyspeck, cherry leaf spot, and bacterial spot of peach.
The update provides specific fungicide recommendations for managing both bitter rot and Marssonina blotch. For those with fruit present, tank-mixing Aprovia or Omega/Orbus with captan is suggested. For growers without fruit or with light crops who wish to be conservative with sprays at this time, switching to captan or micronized sulfur is recommended. The report cautions that alternate row middle sprays should be kept at short intervals: “The longer the interval is to cover the other side of the tree, the longer that side is without fungicide.”
Bitter rot has been identified as one of the most significant threats in recent years for apple growers in eastern United States regions such as Pennsylvania. Research indicates that spores are available throughout the season within buds and mummified fruit left on trees. “Fungicides must be applied before spores infect,” according to guidance provided in the update. Recommendations also emphasize rotating FRAC groups during applications to manage resistance issues.
For organic producers or those seeking alternative controls, options such as micronized sulfur (with caution due to potential russeting), Serenade products, Double Nickel LC, OSO 5%SC, Regalia tank mixes, and potassium phosphite products are mentioned as providing varying levels of protection against bitter rot under different conditions.
Management advice extends beyond apples; stone fruits like peaches are also facing increased risk from bacterial spot under current weather patterns. Growers are urged to maintain copper-based management programs until three weeks before harvest and rotate among labeled products.
Additional resources—including Penn State’s Tree Fruit Production Guide—are available for commercial growers seeking further information about local weather monitoring tools like NEWA stations across Pennsylvania. Penn State Extension continues its mission by delivering science-based education on agriculture through county offices and digital platforms across Pennsylvania counties, according to the official website .
